title: Three Ratios in a Right Triangle

steps.body: Stand at an acute angle θ of a right triangle. The side across from you is the **opposite**; the side touching you (not the hypotenuse) is the **adjacent**; the longest side, across from the right angle, is the **hypotenuse**. Three ratios of these sides get names: **sin θ = opp/hyp, cos θ = adj/hyp, tan θ = opp/adj** — SOH-CAH-TOA.

widget.prompt: Drag the acute angle to 37° and read the opp/hyp card — then resize the whole triangle and watch whether that reading moves.
widget.successFeedback: opp/hyp ≈ 0.6 at 37°, and resizing changed nothing. That is the entire reason sine can be a function of the ANGLE alone: the 3-4-5 triangle and the 6-8-10 triangle are the same shape, so they hand back the same ratio.
widget.lowFeedback: The angle is under 37° — the opposite side is too short relative to the hypotenuse.
widget.highFeedback: The angle is over 37° — the opposite side is too long relative to the hypotenuse.
widget.scaleFeedback: Resize the triangle at least twice before checking. One reading at one size proves nothing about every similar triangle.

explanationVariants: θ sits opposite the 5, so the ADJACENT leg is 12 and cos θ = 12/13: n = 12.
CAH: cosine pairs the adjacent with the hypotenuse.

widget.prompt: In a 5-12-13 right triangle, θ is opposite the side of length 5. Then cos θ = n/13 — what is n?

commonErrors.feedback: 5 is the OPPOSITE side — that's sine's numerator. Cosine takes the adjacent: 12.
13 is the hypotenuse — it's already on the BOTTOM of the ratio. The top is the adjacent leg, 12.

steps.body: Move to the OTHER acute angle and the legs swap jobs: what was opposite becomes adjacent and vice versa — the hypotenuse never moves. That swap is why **sin θ = cos(90° − θ)**: one angle's opposite is its complement's adjacent.

widget.prompt: In the 3-4-5 triangle, let φ be the OTHER acute angle (the one opposite the 4). What is sin φ?

options.feedback: Right — from φ's corner the 4 is the opposite side, and the hypotenuse is still 5.
3/5 is sin θ — from φ's corner the 3 is now ADJACENT. The legs swap jobs when you switch corners.
The hypotenuse is the longest side, so it never sits on the bottom of sine — sin of any acute angle stays below 1.
3/4 pairs the two LEGS — that's a tangent, not a sine. Sine always uses the hypotenuse.

explanationVariants: Opposite = across from θ; adjacent = touching θ but not the hypotenuse; hypotenuse = across from the right angle, always the longest.
Two clues point at the hypotenuse: facing the right angle, and being longest.

widget.prompt: Sort each description by the side it names (relative to the marked angle θ).

items.label: the side across from θ
items.feedback: Across from the angle IS the definition of opposite.

items.label: the side touching θ that isn't the hypotenuse
items.feedback: Touching the angle without being the hypotenuse — that's the adjacent leg.

items.label: the side across from the right angle
items.feedback: The right angle is the biggest angle, and the side facing it is the hypotenuse.

items.label: the longest side
items.feedback: The longest side always faces the largest angle — the 90° corner. Hypotenuse.

widget.missFeedback: Anchor everything to the marked angle: across, touching, or facing the right angle.
widget.successFeedback: Side names locked — every ratio in this course is built from these three.

steps.body: Why do the ratios deserve names? **Scale the triangle and they don't change.** Double 3-4-5 into 6-8-10: the sides all doubled, but opp/adj is still 6/8 = 3/4. Similar triangles share every ratio — so sin, cos, and tan depend only on the ANGLE. Tan even has a physical reading: rise over run, the steepness.

widget.prompt: In the doubled triangle 6-8-10 (opposite 6, adjacent 8), what is tan θ as a decimal?

commonErrors.feedback: 1.5 mixes triangles — 6 over the ORIGINAL's 4. Within 6-8-10, tan θ = 6/8 = 0.75, unchanged by the scaling.
0.6 is 6/10 — sine. Tangent pairs opposite with ADJACENT: 6/8 = 0.75.

explanationVariants: Pythagorean recall: 17² − 8² = 289 − 64 = 225, so the leg is 15 — then tan θ = 8/15.
Legs come from SUBTRACTING squares under the root when the hypotenuse is known.

widget.prompt: A right triangle has hypotenuse 17 and one leg 8. Before any ratio, find the other leg.

commonErrors.feedback: 19 ≈ √(17² + 8²) — squares ADDED. The 17 is the hypotenuse, so the leg comes from subtracting: √(289 − 64) = 15.
9 is 17 − 8 — lengths subtracted directly. The theorem subtracts SQUARES: √(289 − 64) = 15.

widget.fallbackFeedback: √(17² − 8²) = √225 = 15 — and now tan θ = 8/15 for the angle opposite the 8.

hints: The 17 faces the right angle — it's the hypotenuse, so a² + b² = 17².
b = √225 — and once you have it, all three ratios of the triangle unlock.

takeaways: Opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse — all named relative to YOUR angle.
SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj.
Similar triangles share ratios — sin, cos, tan depend only on the angle.
steps.teaser: Next: turning these ratios into a tool — solving for unknown sides.

concept.body: One triangle, three reads. In the 3-4-5 triangle with θ opposite the 3: sine reads opp/hyp = 3/5, cosine reads adj/hyp = 4/5, tangent reads opp/adj = 3/4. Each name just picks a different PAIR of sides.

explanationVariants: The adjacent (4) touches θ; the hypotenuse (5) is the longest side.

widget.prompt: In the 3-4-5 triangle (opposite 3, adjacent 4), what is cos θ as a decimal?

commonErrors.feedback: 0.6 is 3/5 — sine's pair. Cosine takes the ADJACENT over the hypotenuse: 4/5 = 0.8.
0.75 is 3/4 — tangent's pair of legs. Cosine uses the hypotenuse on the bottom: 4/5 = 0.8.
